content: The studies reviewed focused on the effectiveness of different personal protective equipment (PPE) protocols, particularly in the context of preventing contamination during donning and doffing procedures. The findings are as follows: 1. Chughtai et al. (2018) conducted a simulation study to evaluate 10 different PPE donning and doffing protocols recommended by various health organizations for Ebola. Ten participants were randomly assigned to use three different protocols. After donning PPE, fluorescent lotion and spray were applied to simulate contamination, and ultraviolet (UV) light was used to detect fluorescent patches on the skin after doffing. Two protocols where eye protection was worn under head/neck protection (e.g., WHO protocol with coverall and N95) resulted in four large contamination patches but no small patches. Eight protocols where eye protection was worn over head/neck protection (e.g., North Carolina protocol with coverall and N95) showed one large patch on the forehead and one on the forearm. Two protocols (e.g., CDC protocol with coverall and N95, and Health Canada protocol with gown and N95) showed small contamination patches. 2. Suen et al. (2018) conducted an experimental study with 59 participants who performed PPE donning and doffing. Fluorescent solution was applied to PPE surfaces to simulate contamination, and contamination was assessed by counting fluorescent stains on clothing and the environment. PPE 1 (neck-to-ankle outfit, N95 respirator, hood, disposable face shield, surgical gown, boots, and double gloves) had the face shield worn over the head cover. One small contamination patch was observed on the face. PPE 2 (head-to-ankle coverall, N95 respirator, hood, disposable face shield, boots, and double gloves) had the face shield worn under the hood. Four small contamination patches were observed on the face. Neither PPE 1 nor PPE 2 showed large contamination patches on the face. 3. Poller et al. (2018) conducted a simulation study and consensus panel to identify a unified PPE ensemble for high-consequence infectious diseases (HCID) in the UK. A mannequin was used to expose healthcare workers (HCWs) to synthetic bodily fluids (e.g., vomit, sweat, diarrhea, and cough) containing fluorescent tracers visible under UV light. HCWs were examined for contamination after exposure and PPE doffing. Significant contamination events were observed after doffing, often due to protocol failures or complications. The consensus PPE ensemble tested in the study showed no contamination events. 4. Certainty of Evidence: The evidence quality was generally low due to serious indirectness (e.g., reliance on simulation studies and surrogate outcomes like fluorescent contamination rather than actual infection rates) and serious imprecision (e.g., small sample sizes). There was no serious publication bias or inconsistency noted. 5. Key Findings: Eye protection worn under head/neck covering may not significantly reduce contamination compared to wearing it over head/neck covering. The studies were unable to determine whether eye protection worn under head/neck covering improves or worsens contamination or infection outcomes. The results highlight the need for further research with larger sample sizes and real-world infection data to establish definitive conclusions. These findings emphasize the importance of refining PPE protocols to minimize contamination risks during donning and doffing, particularly in high-risk infectious disease settings.
